scenes.heading: The Silk Road: Trade, Ideas, and Decline
scenes.subheading: How did the Silk Road shape Eurasia?
scenes.narration: For over 1,500 years, a vast network of routes stitched Eurasia together from China to Europe.
It began in 130 B.C.E. when China's Han Dynasty officially opened trade with western neighbors.
Chinese silk became a luxury craze in Rome, Egypt, and Greece, giving the network its name.
Caravans also hauled spices, gold, precious stones, and porcelain across deserts and mountains.
The roads linked the Roman, Parthian, Kushan, and Han Empires by both land and sea routes.
Buddhism, Islam, and Christianity traveled into China alongside merchants on these paths. Paper, printing, and gunpowder knowledge moved westward the same way.
Activity peaked in the seventh through ninth centuries as cultures, languages, and technologies blended widely.

lines: New sea routes replaced overland paths
scenes.narration: New sea routes offered safer, cheaper shipping and slowly replaced the difficult overland paths.
Shrinking glaciers and drying water sources also doomed many oasis towns along the route.
The Ottoman Empire closed western trade in 1453 C.E., ending the old network.

checks.original: For over 1,500 years, a vast network of routes stitched Eurasia together from China to Europe.
It began in 130 B.C.E. when China's Han Dynasty officially opened trade with western neighbors.
Chinese silk became a luxury craze in Rome, Egypt, and Greece, giving the network its name.
Caravans also hauled spices, gold, precious stones, and porcelain across deserts and mountains.
The roads linked the Roman, Parthian, Kushan, and Han Empires by both land and sea routes.
Buddhism, Islam, and Christianity traveled into China alongside merchants on these paths.
Paper, printing, and gunpowder knowledge moved westward the same way.
Activity peaked in the seventh through ninth centuries as cultures, languages, and technologies blended widely.
New sea routes offered safer, cheaper shipping and slowly replaced the difficult overland paths.
Shrinking glaciers and drying water sources also doomed many oasis towns along the route.
The Ottoman Empire closed western trade in 1453 C.E., ending the old network.
The Silk Road shaped Eurasia by moving goods, faiths, and technologies across continents for fifteen centuries.

facts.text: The term Silk Road was coined by the 19th-century German explorer Baron Ferdinand von Richthofen (1833–1905).
facts.quote: The term Silk Road (die Seidenstrasse) was first coined by the nineteenth-century German explorer Baron Ferdinand von Richthofen (1833-1905).

facts.text: The Silk Road refers to ancient trading routes stretching across Eurasia from China to Europe.
facts.quote: It broadly describes the ancient trading routes stretching across the Eurasian continent from China to Europe.

facts.text: Silk was one of the earliest and most important commodities traded on the Silk Road.
facts.quote: While silk was clearly one of the earliest and most important commodities traded along the route

facts.text: Precious metals and stones, spices, porcelain, and textiles were also traded along the Silk Road.
facts.quote: precious metals and stones, spices, porcelain, and textiles also traveled the road.

facts.text: Technologies such as silk production, paper making, gunpowder manufacture, and block printing spread westward across Asia via the Silk Road.
facts.quote: The technologies of silk production, paper making, gunpowder manufacture, and block printing made their way west across Asia via this highway.

facts.text: Buddhism, Islam, and Christianity entered China through the Silk Road.
facts.quote: Buddhism, Islam, and Christianity entered China via the Silk Road.

facts.text: The Silk Road connected the Roman, Parthian, Kushan, and Han Empires.
facts.quote: Roman, Parthian, Kushan, and Han Empires alongside the trade routes of the Silk Road.

facts.text: Overland routes crossed the empires and maritime routes crossed the Mediterranean, Indian Ocean, and South China Sea.
facts.quote: red lines marking overland routes and blue lines marking maritime routes across the Mediterranean, Indian Ocean, and South China Sea.

facts.text: Silk production occurred in Tang Dynasty China during the eighth century CE.
facts.quote: Silk production in Tang Dynasty China, eighth century CE.

facts.text: Sailing technology that reached Europe via the Silk Road made Christopher Columbus's voyages possible.
facts.quote: Christopher Columbus's voyages wouldn't have been possible without sailing technology that arrived in Europe along the Silk Road.

facts.text: Silk Road activity peaked during the seventh, eighth, and ninth centuries.
facts.quote: Activity along the Silk Road was at its height in the seventh, eighth, and ninth centuries

facts.text: The Silk Road declined gradually after its peak, not from a single event.
facts.quote: the road slowly began to decline. This decline, however, was not caused by one single event.

facts.text: The development of new sea routes was the most significant factor in the Silk Road's decline.
facts.quote: the development of a new sea route being the most significant. The sea route would supplant the Silk Road.

facts.text: Sea routes offered safer and more economical trade options than overland paths.
facts.quote: One of the most critical shifts was the emergence of sea routes that offered safer and more economical trade options

facts.text: Environmental changes like shrinking glaciers and reduced water sources contributed to the decline of towns along the route.
facts.quote: Environmental changes, particularly the reduction of water sources due to shrinking glaciers, also contributed to the decline of towns along the route.

facts.text: Merchants on the Silk Roads had to learn the languages and customs of the regions they crossed in order to negotiate successfully.
facts.quote: merchants had to learn the languages and customs of the regions they crossed in order to negotiate successfully

facts.text: Knowledge in science, arts, literature, craftsmanship, and technological innovation circulated widely along the Silk Roads.
facts.quote: Knowledge in the fields of science, the arts and literature, as well as craftsmanship and technological innovation, circulated widely

facts.text: Languages, religions, and cultures developed and influenced one another through Silk Road exchanges.
facts.quote: languages, religions and cultures developed and influenced one another

facts.text: In the nineteenth century, archaeologists, geographers, and explorers from France, England, Germany, Russia, and Japan traveled the Silk Roads for discovery.
facts.quote: In the nineteenth century, a new kind of traveller ventured onto the Silk Roads: archaeologists, geographers and explorers driven by a spirit of discovery. Coming from France, England, Germany, Russia and Japan

facts.text: These 19th-century scholars crossed the Taklamakan Desert in western China (present-day Xinjiang) to explore ancient sites.
facts.quote: these scholars crossed, among other regions, the Taklamakan Desert in western China (present-day Xinjiang) to explore the ancient sites along these routes

facts.text: The legacy of the Silk Roads is reflected in distinct but interconnected cultures, languages, customs, and religions that developed over millennia across Eurasia.
facts.quote: the long-standing and ongoing legacy of this remarkable network is reflected in the many distinct but interconnected cultures, languages, customs and religions that have developed over millennia along these routes

facts.text: The Silk Road was a network of routes used by traders for more than 1,500 years.
facts.quote: a network of routes used by traders for more than 1,500 years

facts.text: Trade on the Silk Road began when the Han dynasty of China opened trade in 130 B.C.E.
facts.quote: from when the Han dynasty of China opened trade in 130 B.C.E.

facts.text: Trade on the Silk Road ended in 1453 C.E. when the Ottoman Empire closed off trade with the West.
facts.quote: until 1453 C.E., when the Ottoman Empire closed off trade with the West

facts.text: The term "Silk Road" was first used by German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen in 1877 C.E.
facts.quote: Ferdinand von Richthofen first used the term “silk road” in 1877 C.E.

facts.text: The term "Silk Road" describes the well-traveled pathway of goods between Europe and East Asia.
facts.quote: to describe the well-traveled pathway of goods between Europe and East Asia

facts.text: Some historians prefer the term "Silk Routes" because it reflects the many paths taken by traders.
facts.quote: some historians favor the term Silk Routes because it better reflects the many paths taken by traders

facts.text: The Silk Road originated in the 2nd century BCE during China's Han Dynasty.
facts.quote: The Silk Road is believed to have originated in the 2nd century BCE, during the Han Dynasty in China.

facts.text: Chinese traders first used the route to exchange goods with western neighbors including the Roman Empire.
facts.quote: It was initially used by Chinese traders to exchange goods with their neighbors to the west, including the Roman Empire at the far western end.

facts.text: Chinese silk was highly desired in Rome, Egypt, and Greece.
facts.quote: Chinese silk was widely sought-after in Rome, Egypt, and Greece.

facts.text: The Silk Road was a network of trade routes connecting Europe and Asia.
facts.quote: The Silk Road was a network of trade routes that stretched across the ancient world, connecting Europe and Asia.

facts.text: The route was named for the lucrative silk trade established in China at the eastern end.
facts.quote: It was named for the lucrative silk trade that was established in China at the far eastern end of the trade route.

facts.text: Besides silk, the route transported spices, gold, and precious stones.
facts.quote: Besides silk, the route was also used to transport other goods such as spices, gold, and precious stones.
